analogy.p: Think of energy as the volume of water needed to fill a pool. A garden hose and a fire hose can both fill the same pool, so the total volume (energy) is identical, but the fire hose delivers many more litres every second, so it has a far greater **power**, and the pool fills in less time. The flow rate in litres per second matches watts, which are joules per second. The analogy breaks down because real energy is not a fluid that is physically stored in a container, and some energy is always wasted to the surroundings.

bullets: Symbol **P**; unit the **watt (W)**.
**1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s)**: a 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second.
Power is a **rate**, like speed is the rate of change of distance: the bigger the power, the faster the energy transfer.
Do not confuse **power** (J/s) with **energy** (J) or **force** (N): the unit and the idea are different.
A higher power rating means a device transfers energy faster, so it will usually also **use up energy faster** from its supply.
Typical values: LED lamp about 10 W, laptop about 50 W, kettle about 2 kW, a small car engine tens of kW.
core.p: **Power** is **the rate at which energy is transferred** or **the rate at which work is done**. Two devices can transfer the same total amount of energy, yet the more powerful one does it in less time. Power therefore tells you how quickly a device transfers energy, not how much energy it transfers in total. This is why a 3000 W kettle boils water faster than a 1000 W kettle even though both need the same total energy to reach 100°C.

bullets: **P = E / t**: P in watts (W), E in joules (J), t in seconds (s).
**P = W / t**: P in watts (W), W in joules (J), t in seconds (s). Work done and energy transferred are both measured in joules.
Rearranged: **E = P t** (energy transferred) and **t = E / P** (time taken).
Rearranged for work: **W = P t** and **t = W / P**.
Never forget to convert minutes and hours to **seconds** (1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s).
Remember that a **gradient of an energy–time graph is power**: the steeper the line, the greater the power.
core.h: The equations: power = energy transferred ÷ time and power = work done ÷ time
core.p: The spec gives two forms of the same idea. Because work done is a measure of energy transferred (when a force moves an object, energy is transferred), the two equations are equivalent: **power = energy transferred / time, P = E / t** and **power = work done / time, P = W / t**. In both, the top line is in joules and the time is in seconds. You should be able to apply and rearrange either equation, and convert units where necessary.

bullets: To go from kW to W, **multiply by 1000**; from W to kW, **divide by 1000**.
Worked check: a 2.4 kW kettle on for 3 minutes transfers 2400 x 180 = **432 000 J** (432 kJ).
Mixed units are the commonest trap: always write out the converted values in a line before you substitute.
core.p: Exam questions often give power in kilowatts (kW) or megawatts (MW) because real devices have large ratings. The equations only work in base units (W, J, s), so convert first. Quoting the conversion on the page earns method marks and protects you from losing the answer to a factor of 1000.

bullets: **Work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force, W = F s**.
Weight **W = m g** (g = gravitational field strength, 9.8 N/kg on Earth, or 10 N/kg if the question says so).
Lifting a mass m through a height h: **work done = m g h**, which equals the gain in **gravitational potential energy**.
Power of the lifter: **P = m g h / t**.
The **same job done faster needs more power**: halve the time and the power doubles.
In real machines the motor must also supply energy that is wasted (friction, heating), so the output power is less than the input power.
core.h: Work done and power in lifting and moving things
core.p: When a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, **work is done** and energy is transferred. For lifting an object at a steady speed, the energy transferred is the gain in gravitational potential energy, so the work done is **weight x height = m g h**. Dividing by the time taken gives the power of the person or motor doing the lifting. This is a favourite exam context, such as a crane, a motor lifting a load, or a student running up stairs.

bullets: A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J every second from the electrical supply to the thermal energy stores of the water.
Energy transferred in 1 hour by a 60 W filament lamp: 60 x 3600 = **216 000 J**; by a 10 W LED: 10 x 3600 = **36 000 J**.
The LED is not 'more powerful' at lighting a room; it has a lower power rating, meaning it transfers energy more slowly, but it can produce a similar brightness because it is more **efficient**.
A higher power appliance running for the same time costs more energy; a low-power appliance left on for a long time can still use a lot of energy.
Link to 4.2: **P = V I** and **P = I² R**; energy transferred **E = V I t**, **E = Q V**.
Link to the **kilowatt-hour** (kWh): the energy used by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour (covered in 4.2).
core.p: Every electrical appliance has a **power rating** printed on it, which tells you how many joules it transfers each second when operating normally. Because energy transferred is power x time, you can compare appliances: a higher-rated device transfers more energy in the same time. This links to the electricity topics, where P = V I and P = I² R are used, and to the idea that appliances are chosen for the speed at which they transfer energy to their useful store.

bullets: **Stairs:** a 500 N person climbing 3.0 m does 500 × 3.0 = 1500 J of work whether they walk (10 s, 150 W) or run (5 s, 300 W).
**Kettles:** a 3 kW and a 1 kW kettle both need the same energy to boil the same water, but the 3 kW one transfers it three times as fast, so it takes one third of the time.
**Light bulbs:** a 60 W filament lamp and a 10 W LED can give similar brightness, but the LED transfers energy more slowly because it wastes less as heat.
**Cars:** two cars gain the same kinetic energy reaching 20 m/s, but the one with the more powerful engine gets there sooner.
Halving the time for the same energy **doubles the power**; this is P = E ÷ t with E unchanged.
The graph picture: for the same final energy, the steeper energy–time line is the more powerful.
In an answer say both ideas: **same energy**, **different time**, so **different power**.
core.h: Same energy, different time: examples that show power
core.p: The specification asks you to **give examples that illustrate the idea that the same amount of energy can be transferred in different amounts of time**. In every example the total energy is fixed by the job, such as lifting a person up a flight of stairs or heating a litre of water to boiling, but the time taken depends on how powerful the device or person is. Power therefore tells you how fast the same energy is moved from one store to another. Two people climbing the same stairs gain the same gravitational potential energy, yet the one who runs transfers it in less time and so has the larger power.

bullets: Device A transfers 1800 J in 6 s: P = 1800 / 6 = **300 W**.
Device B transfers 2400 J in 10 s: P = 2400 / 10 = **240 W**.
So A is more powerful even though B transfers more total energy, because A transfers energy faster.
If two machines do the **same work**, the one that takes **less time** has the greater power.
If two machines work for the **same time**, the one that does **more work** has the greater power.
Give the numerical values and a conclusion in a sentence to earn the final mark.
core.h: Comparing powers: which device is more powerful?
core.p: Comparison questions give you two situations and ask which has the greater power. The correct approach is to calculate **energy (or work) divided by time** for each, using seconds, and compare the answers. Do not just look at the larger energy or the shorter time on its own, because power depends on both together.

bullets: **Gradient = ΔE / Δt = power** (in W if E is in J and t in s).
Draw a **large right-angled triangle** on the straight part of the line, then divide the vertical side by the horizontal side.
A horizontal line means no energy is being transferred (power is zero).
Compare two lines: the steeper line is the **more powerful** device.
The **area** under a power–time graph is the energy transferred (a possible Higher-tier skill, since E = P t).
Check axes labels and units before calculating: kJ or minutes on the axes mean you must convert.
core.p: A graph of **energy transferred (y-axis) against time (x-axis)** has a gradient equal to the power, because gradient = change in y / change in x = ΔE / Δt. A straight line means constant power; a steeper line means greater power; a curve that gets steeper means power is increasing. You may be asked to calculate the gradient using a triangle on the line, using large triangles to improve accuracy.

bullets: Efficiency has no unit and is given as a decimal or percentage (multiply the decimal by 100).
Worked idea: a 500 W motor that is 60% efficient has a useful output power of 0.60 x 500 = **300 W**.
The remaining **200 W** is wasted, mainly as thermal energy in the surroundings.
Energy is **conserved**: input power = useful output power + wasted power.
Reducing wasted energy (lubrication, insulation, better design) increases efficiency and reduces the power needed for the same job.
Efficiency can never be greater than 100%.
core.p: Not all the energy a device takes in becomes useful. **Efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer**, and the same ratio works with powers: **efficiency = useful power output / total power input**. A device may have a high input power but a low useful output because energy is wasted, usually by heating the surroundings. Knowing this lets you work out useful power from a given input power and efficiency.

bullets: **Kettle:** energy = m c Δθ, then time = energy / power (links to specific heat capacity).
**Lift or crane:** work done = m g h (= gain in gravitational potential energy), then power = work / time.
**Cyclist or runner:** work done against resistive forces = force x distance, then power = work / time.
**Power station:** output power of 500 MW means 500 million joules transferred every second.
**Energy bill:** the supplier measures the energy transferred over time (kWh).
If a question gives power and time, think **E = P t** immediately; if it gives energy and power, think **t = E / P**.
core.h: Power in everyday and exam contexts
core.p: Power calculations appear in many contexts: electric kettles, lifts, cranes, cyclists, car engines and power stations. In all of them the same two ideas apply: identify the energy transferred (or work done) and the time taken, then use P = E / t. Spotting the right energy calculation first is often the hardest step and is worth practising.

bullets: Combine **E = P t** with **ΔE = m c Δθ** to find the time to heat a substance.
Combine **W = m g h** with **P = W / t** to find the power needed to lift a load.
Combine **efficiency** with power to find useful output power or total input power.
Carry full calculator values through the steps and round only at the end (to a sensible number of significant figures).
State assumptions such as 'assuming no energy is wasted' when you ignore losses.
A comparison of two devices should mention **power rating**, **time taken**, **energy used** and (if given) **efficiency or cost**.
core.h: Higher tier thinking and common exam extensions
core.p: At Higher tier, questions often combine power with other equations in several steps and expect you to carry values through carefully without rounding too early. You may also be asked to evaluate which of two devices is better for a task, which requires you to weigh power, cost, efficiency and time. Showing each step clearly is essential for multi-step questions.

exam: **Define (1 mark):** power is the rate at which energy is transferred (or work is done); say 'rate' and 'energy' or 'work'.
**Unit statement (1 mark):** 1 watt = 1 joule per second; write the unit W.
**Calculations (2–3 marks):** write the equation, rearrange if needed, substitute converted values (seconds, joules, watts), then answer with unit. Show the conversion line separately.
**Multi-step (4–5 marks):** first find the energy (m c Δθ or m g h), then use P = E / t; do not round until the end.
**Comparison questions:** calculate power for both and state which is bigger and why (transfers energy faster).
**Graph questions:** use a large triangle on the straight line; gradient = power; include units.
**Explain with a 'because':** a higher-power appliance transfers more energy each second, so it heats the water in less time.
**Do not claim** that a higher power rating means more efficient; efficiency is separate.
**'Show that' questions:** give the unrounded result and the rounded value.
**Link statements:** work done = energy transferred, so W = Pt as well as E = Pt.
**Check sizes:** a kettle is about 2 kW, so an answer of 20 W or 20 MW is probably a conversion error.

mistakes.r: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, in joules per second.
mistakes.w: Saying power is 'how much energy' a device uses.

mistakes.r: Convert to seconds before using P = E / t.
mistakes.w: Leaving the time in minutes or hours.

mistakes.r: Convert 2.4 kW to 2400 W first, giving 432 000 J.
mistakes.w: Using kW as if it were W (for example 2.4 x 180 = 432).

mistakes.r: Compare work divided by time; the machine that does the work faster is more powerful.
mistakes.w: Saying the machine that does more work is always more powerful.

mistakes.r: The unit is the watt, W (J/s).
mistakes.w: Writing the unit of power as 'joules' or 'watts per second'.
Using mass in grams in W = m g h.

mistakes.r: Efficiency is a ratio with no unit, never greater than 1 (100%).
mistakes.w: Giving efficiency as more than 100% or with a unit.

mistakes.r: A steeper line means a larger gradient, so a greater power.
mistakes.w: Reading a steeper energy–time graph as less power.

mistakes.r: Power is the **rate** of transfer; a lower-power device left on for longer can transfer more total energy (E = P t).
mistakes.w: The more powerful device always transfers more energy in total.

summary: You must define power as the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, use P = E / t and P = W / t (with rearrangements and unit conversions between W, kW and MW), and apply them to lifting, electrical appliances and graphs. It matters because power links energy, time and efficiency and appears in many Paper 1 calculations.

terms.d: The rate at which energy is transferred or the rate at which work is done.
The unit of power; 1 watt is a rate of energy transfer of 1 joule per second.
The amount of energy moved from one store to another, measured in joules (J).
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance; W = F s.
The unit of energy and work done.
The maximum power at which an appliance is designed to operate; it shows the energy transferred each second.
The energy stored in an object because of its height above the ground; Ep = m g h.
Useful output energy transfer divided by total input energy transfer (or useful power divided by total power).
Change in y divided by change in x on a graph; on an energy–time graph it equals power.
Energy that is not usefully transferred, usually dissipated to the surroundings.
The force per unit mass on an object in a gravitational field, 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
How quickly something changes or happens; the change per unit time.
A diagram in which the width of each arrow shows the amount of energy or power; the input splits into useful and wasted parts.
A unit of energy: the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour (3 600 000 J).
The force of gravity on an object, W = m g, measured in newtons (N).

worked.q: A motor lifts a 20 kg load through 3.0 m in 5.0 s. Calculate the power output of the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg) (4 marks)
steps: Work done = force x distance = 196 x 3.0 = 588 J.
